lending-to-known-thieves.title_asserts: The big lenders went on financing dictators while knowing those rulers were stealing the money.
lending-to-known-thieves.why: Two episodes are documented at the institutions' own level: Blumenthal's leaked IMF report on Zaire in 1982 and the World Bank's own August 1997 Jakarta staff memo, with lending continuing in both. What is not documented is the plural claim in the title, that this was how lenders generally dealt with long-ruling allies; nothing opened establishes the practice beyond these cases, and no lender has admitted lending in the knowledge of theft.

settled_by.what_it_is: Christian Science Monitor report on the leaked Blumenthal report, giving Zaire's $4.1 billion debt and his conclusion
settled_by.what_it_establishes: An IMF-sent official told creditors in writing there was "no - I repeat no - chance" of repayment, blaming the corruption of those in power; the report was leaked in Brussels.

settled_by.what_it_is: Wall Street Journal report on the World Bank's August 1997 Indonesia staff memo (Global Policy Forum mirror)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The Bank's own staff estimated 20-30% of Indonesian development funds were diverted and wrote there was no reason to think Bank projects lost less "as our controls have little practical effect", a month after a Bank vice-president said publicly the Bank knew exactly where its money was going.

settled_by.what_it_is: Probe International, Odious debts, with the post-report lending figures for Zaire
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Over the six years after Blumenthal's report the IMF lent Zaire $600 million, the World Bank $650 million and Western governments nearly $3 billion; the debt was over $13 billion when Mobutu fell.

lending-to-known-thieves.still_open: Whether lending despite recorded internal warnings of theft was standing practice rather than two exposed cases. Only leaks produced both documents; the internal country risk assessments and board papers for Zaire, Indonesia, the Philippines and other long-ruling allies have not been pulled from the lenders' archives, and the entry's own would_settle names exactly that.
lending-to-known-thieves.narrower_title: Lenders went on lending to Zaire and Suharto's Indonesia after their own officials reported the theft

lenders-expect-the-riots.title_asserts: The lenders foresee, and accept in advance, the protests and state violence that their loan conditions set off.
lenders-expect-the-riots.why: The pieces hold and the join does not. Price rises written into lending programmes, the protests that followed and the deaths are documented case by case, and a peer-reviewed literature measures worse repression under adjustment programmes. Foreknowledge rests on one leaked Ecuador strategy and on Stiglitz's account to a reporter, which is a person's claim; that lenders write expected repression into their plans as an acceptable cost is exactly the unproven join, and the quantitative literature on the effect itself is still being re-estimated.

settled_by.what_it_is: Dinkel and Nelson, Are IMF Lending Programs Harmful for Human Rights? (PEIO conference paper)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Re-estimating on 120 countries, 1972-2007, with instruments for non-random selection, it finds a significant negative association between IMF programme participation and respect for physical integrity rights, and preliminary evidence that repression worsens as the number of conditions rises. It establishes the association, not that lenders expected it.

lenders-expect-the-riots.still_open: Intent and foreknowledge. Whether risk sections of programme documents forecast unrest before big price rises, how often, and whether the programme was changed when they did. That count is doable now from published IMF staff reports and World Bank programme documents, which is what the entry says. Beyond it: the US Treasury and board record for the programmes concerned, and whether any lender ever recorded expected repression as a cost worth bearing.

documents_i_opened.what_it_is: Dinkel and Nelson, PEIO paper, Dec 2019, on IMF programmes and physical integrity rights

rescue-money-timed-for-elections.title_asserts: Rescue lending is timed and sized so that governments friendly to the big shareholders stay in office.
rescue-money-timed-for-elections.why: The dates, amounts and one public threat are documented: the 1996 Russian arrangement four months before the vote, the 2018 Argentine programme a year before Macri ran, Trump's own words on the 2025 swap. What the record does not settle is that this is how rescue lending is timed as a practice. The strongest academic result I opened is model-dependent, the Claver-Carone account is a reported remark repeated by senators, and the US Treasury's instructions and board minutes are closed.

settled_by.what_it_is: Dreher, Marchesi and Vreeland, The political economy of IMF forecasts
settled_by.what_it_establishes: On up to 157 countries, 1999-2005, countries voting with the United States at the UN receive lower IMF inflation forecasts as their elections approach. The result is significant in the GMM estimates and not significant at conventional levels in OLS marginal effects; it measures forecast bias, not the timing of money.

rescue-money-timed-for-elections.still_open: Whether approvals and disbursements cluster before elections, and whether that clustering tracks alignment with the largest shareholders. A count across all IMF programmes of approvals and payments in the months before elections, set against voting alignment, would answer it from public data. The decisive non-public records are the US Treasury's voting instructions to its executive director and the board minutes for the 1996 Russian and 2018 Argentine arrangements.

markets-opened-for-subsidized-food.title_asserts: Poor countries' food markets were forced open so that rich countries' subsidized farm exports could take them.
markets-opened-for-subsidized-food.why: The forcing open is documented for Haiti: the rice tariff went from 50 to 3 per cent under an IMF and World Bank adjustment programme, imports took over 80 per cent of the market, and the US president who pushed it told the Senate it was a mistake that "may have been good for some of my farmers in Arkansas". What the title adds, that the conditions were written for rich-country exporters, is purpose, and no negotiating record I could open shows it; Ghana's reversal is attributed to IMF pressure by press reports only.

settled_by.what_it_is: Associated Press, With cheap food imports, Haiti can't feed itself
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Clinton's 10 March 2010 statement to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that the policy "was a mistake"; the 50 per cent Duvalier-era tariff cut to 3 per cent after 1994; 80 per cent of rice eaten in Haiti imported.

settled_by.what_it_is: Type Investigations / Foreign Policy, Subsidizing Starvation
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The 1995 cut from 50 to 3 per cent was part of a structural adjustment programme run by the IMF and the World Bank, and Arkansas farmers received more than $2 billion in direct payments 1995-2011, half of it for rice.

markets-opened-for-subsidized-food.still_open: That the tariff conditions were designed to serve rich-country exporters. Nothing opened shows an exporter or its government asking for a particular food-tariff condition. The lender-by-lender comparison of food-tariff conditions against later import shares by supplier, read with US and EU instructions to their executive directors, is still undone. The Ghana paragraph rests on press attribution of IMF pressure, not on an IMF document.
markets-opened-for-subsidized-food.narrower_title: Loan conditions cut poor countries' food tariffs, and subsidized imports took the market

spying-at-the-negotiating-table.title_asserts: Rich countries spy on poor countries in order to win resource and trade deals.
spying-at-the-negotiating-table.why: The leaked documents published by news organisations settle that signals intelligence has operated inside economic negotiations: GCHQ's interception of delegates at the 2009 London G20, including internet cafes set up for them and real-time call records, and the NSA documents naming Petrobras. They do not settle the title's two added elements. The G20 targets were allies and middle-income states, not poor countries, and the one poor-country resource case, the 2004 bugging of Timor-Leste's cabinet, Australia has never officially confirmed; it is known through a former officer who was himself convicted for disclosing it.

settled_by.what_it_is: NPR's account of the Guardian's 16 June 2013 GCHQ documents
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Documents show GCHQ set up internet cafes to intercept email and log keystrokes at the 2009 G20 in England, monitored BlackBerry traffic and kept real-time tabs on delegates' calls, with reports delivered to officials during the summit.

spying-at-the-negotiating-table.still_open: Whether it is routine, and whether poor countries are targeted for the purpose of winning deals. The spying is authorized under the spying state's own law, so the agencies' records of operations against trade, debt and resource negotiations would have to come out by leak or court order. The count the entry proposes, of negotiations later reopened or challenged on espionage grounds, has not been done.
spying-at-the-negotiating-table.narrower_title: Leaked documents show rich countries' spy agencies inside economic negotiations

advisers-who-profit-from-the-sell-off.title_asserts: The foreign advisers who design privatisations profit from them.
advisers-who-profit-from-the-sell-off.why: One instance is settled by a court: a US district judge found Shleifer and Hay liable for making personal investments in Russia while running the USAID-funded Harvard advisory project, and Harvard paid $26.5 million in 2005 without admitting liability. That is the instance, not the practice. The loans-for-shares paragraph is about Russian bank insiders, not about the foreign advisers, so it does not extend the title, and there is no register of adviser holdings from which a pattern could be read.

settled_by.what_it_is: The Harvard Crimson, Harvard Settles Suit For $26.5 M
settled_by.what_it_establishes: A judge in US District Court had found Shleifer and Hay liable for fraud for personal investments in Russia made while advising the USAID-funded programme, their contracts' conflict-of-interest terms barring such investments; Harvard paid $26.5 million, Shleifer $2 million, Hay $1-2 million, none admitting liability, with a two-year USAID debarment.

advisers-who-profit-from-the-sell-off.still_open: Whether advisers to lender-financed privatisations generally end up among the beneficiaries. Advisory contracts are usually confidential and there is no public register of what advisers, their firms or their families hold in the assets being sold, so the comparison of designers against buyers that the entry proposes cannot yet be made.
advisers-who-profit-from-the-sell-off.narrower_title: Harvard's advisers on Russia's privatisation were found liable for investing in the market they were advising on

development-money-through-tax-havens.title_asserts: Money lent for development passes through tax havens.
development-money-through-tax-havens.why: The documented core sits on the page already. The entry's second paragraph is the documented pattern restated: UNCTAD's $100 billion a year, the IMF economists' 40 per cent of FDI through empty companies, Mauritius among the hosts and Senegal's $257 million treaty termination all appear in offshore-routing-lost-tax. What is distinctive, the IFC's own client list, is a count of the lender's published disclosures rather than a suspicion, and the real open question in the entry, whether the havens cut the tax those countries collect, is the one thing the title does not assert.

settled_by.what_it_is: Oxfam Canada release on the Oxfam briefing The IFC and tax havens
settled_by.what_it_establishes: 51 of the 68 companies the IFC lent to in sub-Saharan Africa in 2015 used tax havens, and those 51 took 84 per cent of the IFC's regional investment; IFC investment in companies using havens rose from $1.20 billion in 2010 to $2.87 billion in 2015.

settled_by.what_it_is: Bretton Woods Project, IFC's (ir-)responsible tax investment policy
settled_by.what_it_establishes: An independent watchdog repeats the 51-of-68 count and records World Bank president Jim Yong Kim saying at the April 2016 meetings that moving state assets to tax havens "can have a tremendous negative effect on our mission".

development-money-through-tax-havens.still_open: Whether the haven structures actually reduce tax paid where these companies operate. The IFC does not publish its clients' country-by-country profits and taxes and does not require clients to show them, so the entry's own test cannot be run from outside. That question, not the routing, is what remains suspected.
development-money-through-tax-havens.left_over_after_the_duplicate: The development lenders themselves. The page's pattern is about cross-border corporate investment in general and says nothing about the IFC's own portfolio; the Oxfam count of IFC clients, the 84 per cent share and the 2010-to-2015 rise are not covered anywhere on the page. Being a count of the IFC's published disclosures, corroborated and not disputed by the IFC on the numbers, that leftover reads as documented rather than suspected, so it belongs beside the existing pattern or as its own documented one, with the uncollected tax left as the open question.

banks-that-bank-the-looters.title_asserts: Western banks knowingly hold money stolen from poor countries.
banks-that-bank-the-looters.why: The episodes and the institutional failings are documented; knowledge is documented for one bank and not for the class. The Senate subcommittee's own wording on Riggs is "turned a blind eye", and Riggs pleaded guilty to failing to report suspicious transactions, not to handling stolen money. The FSA found control weaknesses at 15 of 23 London banks holding Abacha-linked money, which is a finding of failure rather than of knowledge, and it named no bank and prosecuted none. The FinCEN Files show banks moving payments they had themselves flagged as suspicious, which is suspicion, not established theft.

settled_by.what_it_is: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Money Laundering and Foreign Corruption, Riggs Bank case study
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Finding (2), "Turning a Blind Eye": Riggs ran more than 60 accounts and CDs for Equatorial Guinea, its officials and their families, by 2003 its largest relationship with balances and loans approaching $700 million, helped set up offshore shell companies for the president and his sons, took $13 million in cash deposits with few questions, and allowed over $35 million wired out of the oil account to unknown companies in secrecy jurisdictions.

settled_by.what_it_is: US Department of Justice press release on the Riggs guilty plea
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Riggs pleaded guilty to a Bank Secrecy Act violation for systemic failure to report suspicious transactions on accounts of Pinochet and the government of Equatorial Guinea, with a $16 million fine and five years' corporate probation; the prosecutor said Riggs "courted customers who were a high risk" despite warnings from regulators.

settled_by.what_it_is: WealthBriefing report on the FSA's investigation into Abacha-linked accounts
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The FSA's three-month investigation found 23 banks with links to the Abacha family and associates, 15 with severe anti-money-laundering weaknesses, seven put on deadlines to fix them; the FSA said it lacked the power to name them.

banks-that-bank-the-looters.still_open: The word the title turns on. Nothing opened establishes that major banks knowingly take looted state money, or that they do so routinely because it pays. Suspicious-activity reports and the bank records behind them are secret by law, and there is no count of how many accounts of senior officials from poor countries were kept open after being flagged.
banks-that-bank-the-looters.narrower_title: Banks held looted state money: one pleaded guilty, and a regulator found 15 London banks with serious failings

debt-for-nature-deals.title_asserts: Debt-for-nature swaps hand a country's oceans and forests over to foreign financiers.
debt-for-nature-deals.why: The mechanics are documented from the arrangers' and the IMF's own accounts: buy-backs at deep discounts, new bonds issued through offshore or charity-owned vehicles, US development-bank credit enhancement, investment-grade ratings on the new paper and binding multi-decade conservation commitments. The handing over is not. No document I opened shows ownership or control of waters or forests transferred; what is shown is a conservation fund whose board is part non-governmental, a complaint to the IDB's watchdog about information, and fees and insurance costs that are not published.

settled_by.what_it_is: Green Finance Institute case study of Belize's 2021 debt conversion
settled_by.what_it_establishes: A $364 million blue loan from a Nature Conservancy subsidiary let Belize repurchase its $553 million superbond at 55 cents, cut debt by 12 per cent of GDP, and created a commitment to protect 30 per cent of its ocean; the loan was financed by blue bonds Credit Suisse issued, rated Aa2 after US DFC credit enhancement, and sold on to pension funds and insurers.

settled_by.what_it_is: Reuters report on Ecuador's Galapagos buy-back (Stabroek News)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Credit Suisse repurchased $1.6 billion face value of Ecuadorean notes at 53.25, 38.5 and 35.5 cents on the dollar, against the backdrop of an impeachment process, in what it called the biggest debt-for-nature swap struck to date.

debt-for-nature-deals.still_open: What the countries actually net and who decides. Arrangers' fees, insurance premiums and net fiscal savings are unpublished for every swap I looked at; the share of private and non-governmental seats on the Galapagos Life Fund board comes from an advocacy network, Latindadd, not from the fund's own constitution; and the IDB complaint is an allegation about information, with no finding yet.
debt-for-nature-deals.narrower_title: Debt-for-nature swaps arranged by banks, with unpublished fees and conservation funds sitting part outside government

private-courts-for-investors.title_asserts: There are private tribunals that can order countries to pay companies billions of dollars.
private-courts-for-investors.why: As the title stands it asserts nothing open. The tribunals exist by treaty, the awards are published in ICSID's own case database, and this map counts 1,332 treaty cases from UNCTAD's navigator. The documented core, foreign companies using investment treaties to sue states and winning large awards, is already the page's pattern on companies suing the state, which lists the claims and awards case by case and names ICSID as a World Bank Group body. The genuinely open material in the entry is not in its title.

settled_by.what_it_is: ICSID case database, Tethyan Copper Company Pty Limited v. Islamic Republic of Pakistan (ARB/12/1)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: The registry's own record: claim registered 12 January 2012 under the Pakistan-Australia BIT, tribunal of three, award rendered 12 July 2019, then an annulment proceeding. The institution records the case and its outcome; the power to award against a state is not in question.

settled_by.what_it_is: ICSID case database, Occidental Petroleum Corporation and others v. Republic of Ecuador (ARB/06/11)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: Registered 13 July 2006 under the Ecuador-US BIT, award rendered 5 October 2012 with a dissenting opinion attached, followed by annulment proceedings.

settled_by.what_it_is: UNCTAD, Investor-State arbitration under investment laws (IIA Issues Note)
settled_by.what_it_establishes: UNCTAD's own figures for treaty-based ISDS, 38 per cent of concluded cases resolved in favour of the state and about 29 per cent in favour of investors, the comparison the entry uses, and that investors prevailed in 58 per cent of cases decided on the merits.

private-courts-for-investors.still_open: The part the title leaves out and the story carries: that a small group of arbitrators decides most cases and sits on company boards, that the same lawyers arbitrate and act as counsel, and that governments drop or soften regulation under threat of a claim. Those are contested, the 15-arbitrators count comes from an advocacy study whose critics answered it in print, and regulatory chill is unmeasured because nothing records a law not passed.
private-courts-for-investors.left_over_after_the_duplicate: Two things the existing pattern does not touch. First, who the arbitrators are: the 15-arbitrators-55-per-cent count, the board seats and the double-hatting, which stay suspected and are disputed rather than settled. Second, regulatory chill, laws withdrawn or weakened after a threatened claim, which no source quantifies. If the entry stays it needs a title that asserts one of those rather than the existence of the tribunals; mining and oil awards against Pakistan and Ecuador also widen the existing pattern beyond privatized services, so they could simply be added to it.
